summary: Warns Tenex users about a bug in the Tenex FTP: some Tenex programs mark the end of a line with an ASCII Unit Separator, and the FTP user program sent that over the network instead of converting it to carriage return and line feed. Non-Tenex recipients would get garbled line spacing.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 571 warns that some Tenex FTP transfers sent a local line-ending character that other systems did not recognize. It recommends converting the file with TECO before sending it to a non-Tenex site.

questions: why did tenex ftp files look wrong
why did tenex ftp files lose line breaks
what does ascii unit separator mean in rfc 571
subtitle: A warning about Tenex FTP sending the wrong line-ending character.

tldr.problem: Some Tenex programs used ASCII Unit Separator to mark line endings, and the Tenex FTP user sent those characters unchanged to non-Tenex systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says FTP required the Tenex sender to translate those line endings to carriage return and line feed, but the implementation did not do so.
tldr.outcome: A recipient might lose line spacing or treat the file as one long record. The suggested workaround is to load and save the file with TECO before transfer.

today: RFC 571 is a historical warning about a line-ending problem in the Tenex FTP implementation.

sections.title: The Tenex Line-Ending Problem
sections.content:
Some Tenex programs used the ASCII Unit Separator character to mark the end of a line instead of carriage return and line feed. The Tenex FTP user implementation sent Unit Separator characters over the network rather than translating them as the FTP protocol required.

A non-Tenex recipient would not treat these characters as line endings. The RFC gives the example that CCN would treat the file as one very long logical record and fold it into successive 360 records.
sections.plainLanguage: Some Tenex files ended lines with a character that other systems did not treat as a line break. Tenex FTP sent that character without converting it, so the recipient could lose the file's line structure.

sections.title: Converting the File Before Transfer
sections.content: The RFC suggests passing the file through a Tenex program that performs the needed conversion before sending it. It specifically names TECO: loading and saving the file with TECO replaces Unit Separator characters with carriage-return and line-feed sequences. The author notes that other means may also exist.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending the file, use a Tenex program to replace its line-ending characters. The RFC says that loading and saving it with TECO makes this conversion.

sections.title: Who Is Affected
sections.content: The warning concerns transfers from Tenex to a site that does not give special meaning to Unit Separator. The problem is the sender's failure to translate the local line-ending representation into the FTP form, not a claim that every Tenex file or transfer is affected.
sections.plainLanguage: The issue applies when a file contains these Tenex line endings and goes to a system that does not recognize them. Converting the file first avoids relying on the receiver to interpret the Tenex character.
